what.text: Tamoxifen is a non-steroidal anti-estrogen, taken by mouth. It competes with estrogen for binding sites in tissues such as the breast. The label notes it also has some estrogen-like effects, which may explain its effect on the uterus.
How it acts, according to the FDA label:

items.text: In breast cancer cells it competes with estradiol for the estrogen receptor. In rats it blocked and shrank chemically induced breast tumors.
In men with low sperm counts, the label says tamoxifen raised LH, FSH, testosterone and estrogen levels. This is the basis for its off-label use in men.

what.text: Tamoxifen is FDA approved for breast cancer, including metastatic breast cancer in men. Its use in men for breast growth (gynecomastia), testosterone or fertility is off-label.

research.text: Tamoxifen’s approvals rest on large trials in women with breast cancer or at high risk of it. The label adds published data on men with breast cancer. For off-label uses in men, randomized trials have tested it to prevent breast growth caused by the prostate cancer drug bicalutamide, and, combined with testosterone undecanoate, in men with low sperm counts.

research.meta: Published series · label data · Uncontrolled reports
research.title: Men with breast cancer (tamoxifen label)

facts.v: published reports and case reports, no control group

research.found: 66 of 132 men responded, a 50% objective response rate. The label reports this as the basis for treating metastatic breast cancer in men. Loss of libido and impotence led some men to stop.

research.title: Tamoxifen or radiotherapy to prevent breast growth on bicalutamide (Perdonà et al.)

facts.v: 151 men with prostate cancer starting bicalutamide 150 mg a day
bicalutamide alone, bicalutamide plus tamoxifen 10 mg a day, or bicalutamide plus a single dose of breast radiotherapy
breast growth and breast pain; PSA; quality of life

research.found: Breast growth occurred in 35 of 51 men on bicalutamide alone, 4 of 50 with tamoxifen and 17 of 50 with radiotherapy. Breast pain: 29 of 51, 3 of 50 and 15 of 50. This use is off-label.

research.title: Tamoxifen dose-response for bicalutamide breast events (Fradet et al.)

facts.v: 282 men with prostate cancer on bicalutamide 150 mg a day
tamoxifen 1, 2.5, 5, 10 or 20 mg a day, or placebo, for 12 months, then 12 months of bicalutamide alone
breast growth or pain; PSA control

research.found: At 6 months, breast events fell with dose: 96.7% on placebo, 86.2% on 1 mg and 8.8% on 20 mg. PSA control was not affected. After tamoxifen stopped, breast events were common in all groups. Hot flushes rose at 5 mg or more. This use is off-label.

research.title: Tamoxifen plus testosterone undecanoate in low sperm counts (Adamopoulos et al.)

facts.v: 212 men with low sperm counts of unknown cause (idiopathic oligozoospermia) in subfertile couples; 82 men with normal counts as a comparison
tamoxifen 20 mg plus testosterone undecanoate 120 mg a day, or placebo
pregnancies, sperm count, motility and shape

research.found: Total sperm count, motility and normal shape rose on the combination, not on placebo. Spontaneous pregnancies: 33.9% vs 10.3% (36 vs 11). This tested the combination, not tamoxifen alone, and is off-label.

research.text: The label describes large trials in women, including NSABP P-1 in women at high risk of breast cancer. These trials define its serious risks (uterine cancers, stroke, lung clots). They do not tell us about off-label effects in men.
In rats, tamoxifen impaired fertility and conception in females and caused fetal deaths. In rats it blocked and shrank chemically induced breast tumors.

us.text: Tamoxifen is FDA approved, first as Nolvadex in December 1977, for breast cancer. The label covers metastatic breast cancer in women and men. Uses in men for breast growth, testosterone or fertility are off-label. It is not a controlled substance. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: NDA 017970 (AstraZeneca), approved December 30, 1977, is now listed as discontinued. Generic tablets are approved and marketed, and Soltamox, an oral solution, was approved in October 2005 (NDA 021807).

items.text: metastatic breast cancer in women and men; add-on (adjuvant) treatment of breast cancer; ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) after surgery and radiation; and lowering breast cancer risk in women at high risk.
metastatic breast cancer is an approved use. Preventing or treating breast growth from bicalutamide or other causes, raising testosterone and male infertility are off-label.

the label has a boxed warning for women with DCIS and women at high risk of breast cancer: uterine cancers, stroke and pulmonary embolism, some fatal, were more common on tamoxifen in NSABP P-1. It says the benefits outweigh the risks in women already diagnosed with breast cancer.

under section 503A, pharmacies may compound only with bulk substances that meet a USP or NF monograph, are part of an FDA-approved drug, or are on FDA’s 503A bulks list. Tamoxifen citrate is the active ingredient of FDA-approved tablets. A compounded tamoxifen product is not FDA approved.

world.lead: Tamoxifen is an approved breast cancer medicine in the US, Canada, Northern Ireland and all 27 EU member states. Use in men for breast growth, testosterone or fertility is off-label wherever checked. It is banned in sport at all times.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Tamoxifen is named under class S4.2, anti-estrogenic substances (anti-estrogens and SERMs), on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List. S4 is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition), and S4.2 substances are Specified Substances. The ban is not limited to men. Tamoxifen stays named in S4.2 on the 2027 list, in force January 1, 2027.

side.text: The label’s serious risks come from trials in women: uterine cancers, stroke, pulmonary embolism and other blood clots, cataracts and liver effects. In men, the label notes loss of libido and impotence; in the bicalutamide trials, hot flushes rose at higher doses.

items.text: in NSABP P-1, endometrial cancer occurred at 2.20 vs 0.71 per 1,000 women-years on tamoxifen vs placebo; stroke at 1.43 vs 1.00; pulmonary embolism at 0.75 vs 0.25. Some were fatal.
deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are more common on tamoxifen, more so with chemotherapy.
corneal changes, color vision changes, retinal vein clots and retinopathy have been reported. Cataracts and cataract surgery were more common in NSABP P-1.
liver cancer was reported in a few patients in some trials; rarely, fatty liver, cholestasis, hepatitis and liver necrosis have also been reported, a few of them fatal.
the label says the safety profile in men appears similar to that in women. Loss of libido and impotence have led men to stop treatment.
hot flushes were more common at tamoxifen doses of 5 mg or more in the 2007 trial; other side effects were similar across groups.

hot flushes are the most common side effect in metastatic breast cancer. Rarely, raised triglycerides with pancreatitis, severe skin reactions (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome), lung inflammation and allergic swelling have been reported.
it may cause fetal harm. The label tells women not to become pregnant while taking it or for 2 months after stopping.

unconfirmed: The TGA’s register could not be reached, so Australian product registrations were not confirmed.
Great Britain (outside Northern Ireland) was not checked on the MHRA’s own product register.
The year FDA first approved tamoxifen for male breast cancer was not found in the records opened; the current label includes it.
surprises: Male breast cancer is an approved use on the US tamoxifen label (metastatic breast cancer in women and men), based on published uncontrolled reports in 132 men with a 50% response rate.
